lesson.title: A Different Story About Human Nature: The Humanistic Turn
lesson.summary: Humanistic personality theory arose as a deliberate reaction against both psychoanalysis and behaviorism, arguing that people have free will and an innate drive toward growth rather than being ruled by unconscious drives or external conditioning.
lesson.body:
By the middle of the twentieth century, personality psychology was largely split between two dominant, and very different, ways of explaining human beings. Psychoanalysis, built on Freud's ideas covered earlier in this course, portrayed personality as shaped by unconscious drives, buried childhood conflicts, and a constant, largely hidden struggle between the id, ego, and superego. Behaviorism, on the other side, treated internal mental life as largely off limits to science and explained behavior almost entirely through conditioning and reinforcement history, with little room left for conscious choice.

A group of psychologists, most centrally Carl Rogers and Abraham Maslow, pushed back hard against both views. Their objection to psychoanalysis was that it painted an overly pessimistic and deterministic picture of human nature, as if people were essentially prisoners of unconscious drives they could barely control. Their objection to behaviorism was almost the opposite: that it reduced people to passive responders shaped entirely by their environment, denying any real role for conscious thought, free will, or personal meaning. This new movement is often called psychology's third force, positioned deliberately as an alternative to both of the reigning schools.

Humanistic psychology starts from a different set of assumptions. People are seen as innately good and as carrying a natural drive toward growth and toward fulfilling their own potential, rather than being driven mainly by conflict or shaped mainly by outside reinforcement. People are treated as conscious, active agents who make real choices, not simply pawns of hidden drives or environmental conditioning. And rather than focusing on universal drive theories or on observable behavior alone, humanistic psychologists emphasized each person's own subjective experience, how the world feels and looks from the inside, as the most important thing to understand about personality.

The chapters that follow introduce three of the movement's central ideas: Rogers's concepts of unconditional positive regard and self-concept, and Maslow's concept of self-actualization. Humanistic psychology has had a lasting influence, shaping person-centered therapy, humanistic approaches in education, and later work on well-being and human strengths, and it shifted the field's overall tone toward a more optimistic view of human potential. At the same time, it is fair to note a real limitation: concepts like an innate growth tendency or the drive toward self-actualization are hard to define precisely enough to measure and test the way a controlled experiment requires, and critics have argued that humanistic theory sometimes functions more as a philosophy or a set of values than as a strictly testable scientific theory.
